item.title: How I use AI (Oct 2026)
item.description:
How I use AI (Oct 2026)

Wow, things have changed.

Last October, I took stock of how I was using AI — specifically the cool stuff like LLMs that we call 'AI’. I’m so glad I did. Things are very, very different 12 months later.

Background

I still believe I use AI fairly typically, but I’ve had a notable change in background. Last October, I was an engineer on Microsoft’s Windows AI team. I am now a research engineer at Salesforce AI Research. I spend more time supporting scientists & building rapid prototypes, rather than working with a large team of engineers. I spend about ~$3,000/month in tokens.

In any case, I mostly use AI in the same ways as last year:

CodingResearch & searchSummarization & transcription & (new) voiceWritingArt & music & (new) video

Also new this year, I’ve drafted a personal AI policy; we’ll start there.

As before, this remains purely my opinion & speculation. If you use AI differently, let me know!

My AI policy

This year I began drafting a personal AI policy — as in, a document for how I want to use AI in my life. I am very excited about it. I am also working on an explicit AI policy for this site (still thinkin’; probably based on Hank Green’s policy), but a personal policy is to give me a framework for using these tools day-to-day.

AI leaks into life. Teammates ask Claude to write their Slack messages, grandparents generate creepy memes of their grandchildren, and researchers delegate their thinking to machines. I’ve seen all of these things; even strong creators like Hank Green and BrainPOP get lost.

Humans clearly do not have norms for using these tools, and we’re messing up. I hope that a personal policy will ground me as AI becomes smarter. I hope to adapt that policy over time, and I’m eager to see how it evolves. I’m also open to draft 1 being utterly, hopelessly wrong.

Ultimately, I want to spend my life making cool things with other people. AI can help, AI can hurt. A policy helps me find the difference.

Coding

Writing code is solved.

Last year, I waxed poetic about how GitHub Copilot autocomplete transformed how I write code.

Well, uh, I no longer write much code. Agentic coding has made it obsolete.

My workday now means managing ~5–6 Claude Code (or OpenCode or Codex or Pi) agents. I’ll give Claude a feature to implement, or a bug to reproduce, or any other task I used to do by hand; each agent gets its own copy of the code (a Git worktree, if you’re technical), then just… gets to work. The agents write code, run tests, even create & review PRs.

They are nothing short of magic:

They let me build fast: agents will prototype any new feature in ~20 minutes. I truly cannot count the number of features, bugfixes, tests, and tools I’ve (AI’ve?) been able to build because of these agents. For example, AI let me test confusing audio code on macOS and iOS in just a few minutes.

They let me try crazy things: human teams aim to “fail fast”; agents can fail ultra-fast. I’m happy to test crazy new ideas and throw out what doesn’t work well. It was able to wire & test a huge change to Mumble that added better noise cancelling; I use my beta build of it nearly every day.

They remove drudgery: I’ve had agents diagnose & fix urgent bugs with nothing more than a description and a “please fix!” while I continued working on other things.

They let me be kinder: since agents write everything, it is simple to propose sweeping changes to my teammates during code review, or even write my own versions — both things unthinkable in the era of hand-written code.

I do not believe engineering is solved: left to run on their own, agents will build poorly-functioning, over-architected, unreadable, self-congratulatory piles of slop. Every friend I’ve asked agrees that agents still need human taste and experience to produce good work. Some of that is minutiae (like that annoying status dot Claude likes to throw onto sites), but most of it is critical. Agents tend to get lost on their own. My most successful work this year was hand-writing a tool, replacing ~4,000 lines of vibe-code with a few hundred. My system has proven more flexible, easier to test, and more generalizable than what it replaced.

It remains to be seen how long that human edge will last, though.

I also now reckon with the fatigue of using these agents. Managing 6 different conversations with 6 different robots about 6 different features is overstimulating & exhausting in a way that coding never was. When I started using agents, I remember rushing to answer their questions like they were human colleagues waiting for help! While I have tempered that anthropomorphic bias, it’s exhausting to juggle so many problems at once. The allure of sending just one more prompt before lunch… then dinner… oy. There is also, as I wrote in Consider the chairmaker, the decline of craft. My friend Peter laments ceding the joy of programming to machines: for many of us, honing the code, finding the right design, seeing the parts mesh together — that was the meditative purpose we found in our jobs. Now, we rarely write anything. We instead delegate it to agent number 7.

But let me return to the joy of working with agents: they are so fast, so open to feedback, and so intelligent. Working with them can be utterly delightful.

For example, while I was building a harness for voice agents, one programming agent decided (correctly) that my simple test harness was insufficient. So it used my Mac’s built-in text-to-speech to directly test the voice agent it was building. Then, newer agents started doing it, too. Either they had documented the technique, or they were each smart enough to independently discover it. Directly testing the product they were building. Absolutely brilliant.

Agents frequently recommend knobs & settings that I’ll reject for being too complex and unnecessary — and, voilà, I’ll need the knob next week. Silly human!

Anyway, because of agentic coding, agentic pull requests are increasingly the way I review agent code. “Make a draft PR,” I write, “I’ll review it soon!” And review it I do — agents still aren’t reliable enough to trust without validating, so I’ll still review their code & test it manually. However, I don’t do the “line-by-line” code reviews I used to do with humans. I focus instead on architecture, on larger patterns in the code. Are there systemic issues with an approach? Should I add new agent guidance to CLAUDE.md? Can I build better test harnesses, so the machines can test their own code?

Agentic code review is surprisingly helpful here: I try to write rules for the code review robots whenever I notice a recurring issue with generated code, so the agents will identify & fix issues by themselves. One rule I enjoyed creating: a "Claude-y comment detector." You think my writing is verbose? Try Claude’s.

On more typical engineering teams, human code review seems increasingly difficult. A friend of mine complained that his teammates simply ask “their” Claudes to review code written by other Claudes. An ouroboros of Claudes! Agents catch bugs & stylistic issues very well, but they are abysmal at designing architecture. Agentic code review is certainly not a replacement for humans yet.

Last year, I was skeptical of inline editing and code mode, both features of GitHub Copilot. They were not very useful then, and they are even less useful with agents. I have removed them from the table.

UsefulnessNotesAutocomplete👍👍Still great, obsoleteAgent mode👍👍👍The most important use of AI todayAgentic PRs😒Validation loop still slowCode review👍Removes some drudgery, but not human-level yet
Research & search

Last year, I was excited about research & search: they were the most frequent reason I used ChatGPT. Now, generative AI is the default way I do those things.

The biggest change has been Google’s AI summary. Google’s first or second result is almost always an AI summary, and it’s usually decent. So my traditional search is now AI-first by default. Is it perfect? Absolutely not. In one day, it gave me incorrect URLs for NPR’s RSS feeds and couldn’t find the origin of “AI’ve”.

But none of the top results clearly gave me NPR’s RSS feeds either, and even Claude couldn’t find “AI’ve”. Meanwhile, searching “HP Reverb G2” gave me the specs I was looking for, “ai intelligence is spiky” pointed me to the correct term (“jagged”), “emoji sigh” gave me the right emoji without sending me to a scummy site, and “rel nofollow markdown” reminded me how to link that site without giving them search engine juice.

Product search is still mediocre. I’ll look at the summary when I search “best hysa”, but I don’t trust Gemini to have good advice on where to put my money. Claude certainly helped me explore budget VR options and understand technical details about grease for KitchenAid mixers, but can I trust its coffee table recommendations? Sleeper sofas? Let’s not even mention how uncomfortable it is to see ads in my ChatGPT chats.

Pub facts—stuff I’d ask my wife at a pub — remain awesome with LLMs. Again, Google’s AI summary means “lego cat on a balcony tiktok guy” will help me find @avadonye’s precarious LEGO builds, and “art vtuber who is a lizard on TikTok who gives short tutorials” will help me find Mallow, the art vtuber who is a lizard on TikTok who gives short tutorials.

I often avoid using LLMs for pub facts, in the same way I generally avoided Google for them before, because I like puzzling with my friends. I like Fermi problems.

But I’m more and more excited about using LLMs as teachers to explore well-known concepts. I breezed over this last year, but that is unfair to LLMs. I believe they are the greatest teachers humanity has ever created.

I had an LLM walk me step-by-step through fine-tuning Mistral to speak like a pirate (yarrr).I used Claude to practice responding to an EMS call I heard on the radio.I had Claude use a socractic method skill I found via Dan MacKinlay to help me brainstorm new approaches for semantic endpointing (knowing when a user is done speaking) in voice agents.I asked Claude to explain typical approaches to a complex legal document.I’ve even had Claude quiz me on a long code review, to ensure I understood what the agent had written. The open-source project Mumble actually added a similar quiz to their AGENTS.md a few weeks ago.

I am actually jealous of the endless care & patience that these machines show. I hope we discover how to share this patience with our kids while ensuring our kids still learn. Veritasium’s Derek Muller discusses this in What Everyone Gets Wrong About AI and Learning: AI is incredible at drilling repetitive practice, at giving immediate feedback, of all the things a private tutor can do… if you ask it to.

“The world is full of heavy objects,” he says, “and yet most people are not ripped.”

That is my greatest fear with AI tutoring today. That these machines must be reminded to teach. Per Muller, learning requires Type 2 thinking — enaging the slow, reasoning mode of your brain. This is very difficult. Your body will surreptitiously & continuously nudge you out of this mode. Tutors exist to force you back into it. But ChatGPT exists to do things for you: it is so fine-tuned for that use that it tends to forget “it’s meant to be a tutor”, even when previously asked. What learning may occur when you have both forgotten your desire to learn?

This differs from my biggest concern last year: accuracy. Responses then often had basic factual errors, but that seems less of an issue today. I think there are 2 basic factors:

I am more AI-literate. I think more of us have a “sense” of what AI can do well, so we avoid the jagged edges.

I don’t, for example, trust ChatGPT’s ability to read sparsely-digitized documents from 1867. So I asked hopefully, then basically ignored its findings.

AI is smarter. Just like in coding, I think we hit an inflection point this year, where models are simply smart enough to answer more things reliably.

MAJOR spoilers for Control if you click, but there’s a reason Google’s AI summary of its ending (using Gemini 3, from November 2025) is simple and correct while Bing’s (using ~GPT 4o, from May 2024) is not, conflating the game with its sequel.

This trend extends to literature searches. Last year, I shared my trepidation about using LLMs for complex literature searches. My skepticism remains: these machines have access to everything ever written, so they can support any premise in good faith. Also, it is well-demonstrated that LLMs have default bias, politically or in other fields, like business strategy. I am worried about their ability to subtly impose worldview, either on their own or at the behest of corporations and governments.

Yet LLMs are now my first choice for literature searches. That’s partially because Google searches have that AI summary on top, so I end up reading it, but also because LLMs have been much more effective than traditional search at finding good, nuanced data for me — despite potential bias. You must remember that Google Scholar search kinda sucks: when I started researching Car touchscreens are cheap, not good, for months I could not find any studies beyond one done by an auto magazine—Vi Bilägare. That was despite having worked at a Georgia Tech lab that researched car user interfaces! Especially as they’ve gotten smarter & I’ve developed intuition, LLMs are good finders. Just see Claude’s investigation into human perceptions of latency for me:

Ultimately, though, human experts are still more reliable than agents. That’s how I moved forward with “Car touchscreens”—I asked someone from that GT lab. I’ve also been buying more books, even slightly-obsolete ones like Card, Morgan, & Newell’s The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (everyone, including LLMs, cite it) or old editions of Wicken’s Engineering Psychology and Human Performance (via a nuclear consultant I met at a wedding). They ground my research, simply by offering a legible worldview.

And that’s why I’ve been disappointed in AI as collaborator for novel research. AI has harmed some research I’ve been doing.

My team at Salesforce has been working on voice stuff, and I’ve been trying to improve turn detection — understanding when a user is done speaking. That’s a hard problem, and it’s been a great opportunity to read fundamental research on how human conversation works (finally!). AI was great at finding that research and good datasets (though my teammates gave me context the AI never did). And it was great when I asked it to use the Socratic method to help me design my own turn detection model — until, on a whim, I asked: “are there better architectures?” Why yes, yes there were. AI had led me astray.

That’s not the only time AI waylaid me. LLMs could not figure out how to annotate that model’s training data correctly. I spent days going back and forth with them, trying to decide how to separate turns from interruptions. It is embarrassing how simple the problem became after one good discussion with a human teammate. LLMs are not yet good companions when brainstorming complicated things.

It is weird to write this when OpenAI just solved a Millenium Problem, proved a weaker version of another, solved hundreds more, and releases more solutions every day. But those results cost “millions of dollars”: you need to burn tokens, having agents review agents review agents… just to produce something coherent. In my case, I find I enter this “AI fog” where it takes more effort to review the agent’s response than to come up with my own answers.

It is obvious that AI researchers are coming. Just… not today, not with me.

UsefulnessNotesTraditional search👍It’s now my default, and it’s fineProduct search❌Still tasteless & untrustworthyPub facts👍👍Still makes me more annoying at parties!Learning (Explaining well-known concepts)🤔👍Am I just convincing myself I’m learning?Literature searches👍Still can support any claim, but at least it’s not Google Scholar(new) Novel research🤔Coming soon, but not yet
Summarization & transcription & voice

LLMs (and local models!) remain uninterestingly good at summarization & transcription.

I’ve been using OpenWhispr and Handy to dictate to my computer, especially to talk to my agents. The best models on the planet run on your computer locally, for free. My biggest complaint is that the apps have bugs (hotkeys work inconsistently, etc.). It’s hard to describe a more boring type of success.

My meetings have automatic notes. My friend built a local pipeline to transcribe & search his childhood home videos. Vikram Oberoi built a site (in 2024!) that automatically transcribes NYC city hall meetings. You can do all of these things on your Mac.

However, I have yet to reliably use voice beyond dictation.

There’s a reason my team at Salesforce is researching it: voice is the original modality. It should be a seamless way of talking to these human-like robots. But I have never felt compelled to talk to my robots; it’s never been frictionless or private-feeling or useful enough. Does old-school Siri count?

UsefulnessNotesSummarization👍👍Boringly goodTranscription👍👍Great for talking to my coding agents!(new) Voice🤔Seems useful, don’t know how
Writing

Last year: “ew.” This year: “ew.”

I still do not use AI to write from scratch, nor as an outlining aid, for things I make.

I’ve narrowed this rule a bit from last year. Last year, I argued that LLMs always lacked context and so were poor communicators. With agentic coding, that’s changed. So I’ve had agents document experiments I designed but had no hand in executing, or write READMEs for code they generated end-to-end.

But even that limited exception irks me. I do not like when I stumble upon AI-generated spew, so why should I subject others to it? To that end, I’ve started prompting my agents to identify themselves whenever they write prose, and I often end up rewriting their documents myself (or at least adding an executive summary). That has helped, but I’m not certain it is enough.

In general, I’m surprised how bad AI remains at writing. AI writing is demanding to read: usually plodding, repetitive, and vapid — but then randomly terse and vague, like it doesn’t understand its own words. Agents will so often cite & quote & summarize every paper ever published, then synthesize it all into a mound of nonsense. That is the AI fog I hit: do I misunderstand all these new papers, or did the LLM just serve up some pseudo-profound bullshit? It is bewildering to me that these models can solve generational math problems on one hand, yet utterly fail to describe turn-taking behavior in humans on the other. That is, I guess, their jagged intelligence. They do not reason like we do. They cannot be fine-tuned to speak like we do. So they solve problems we cannot, and share them in reports we struggle to understand.

In any case, it should not be surprising that I do not use AI for writing or outlining in my communication; neither at work nor on this blog. My employer pays me for my ideas, which only I can voice. And I write on this blog for fun. Writing is an art and a skill I enjoy pursuing.

Why would I delegate my voice to a machine that writes tedious dreck?

It’s still great for finding words. Google AI talked me out of writing “hawking off” (which is not an expression) instead of “ceding” later on. But I’m tempering my regard for it as an editor. Despite my positive & worried assessment last year, when I spoke to several friends who asked agents to edit their job applications, their feedback was universally tepid. Agents were sycophantic, reluctant to be critical. And anyone who worked around this (by saying, for example, "my friend wrote this") found that agents offered misplaced, trite advice that lacked nuance. The agents seemed to regress to the mean: helping those with the worst writing and hindering those with the best. The agents were… fine.

As one friend put it:

[AI writing] is as good as it was 3 years ago. Which, when you consider how much everything else has changed since then…

I avoided using AI editors altogether this year, out of fear that they would erase my voice. But I’m increasingly certain they would just blandify it. AI tells remain the same as always (“You’re absolutely right!”), and these machines seem incapable of improvement without substantial guidance. Perhaps it’s survivorship bias, but these very smart machines produce very mediocre writing.

UsefulnessNotesWriting from scratch❌Still ewFinding good words👍👍Still goodEditing👍Mediocre. I don’t use it.
Art & music & video

Finally, art. I still don’t have a good use for image generation.

Last year, I used AI to generate a few odds and ends, but I stopped this year, mostly out of a vague sense of discomfort. I felt like I was ceding opportunities for creativity to the mediocrity machine.

I’ve enjoyed a lot of the low-effort memes I’ve seen; We need more data centers is one of my favorite jokes all year. And AI helped design some useful presentations I attended. But I’m not sure how AI art fits into life on Earth. Last year I thought I saw AI art at a gift shop. Well, now I’ve seen AI Sketchers ads, AI event posters, AI restaurant menus, AI logos for stores and e-sports teams, AI canvases at HomeSense, and AI t-shirts at Walmart. It’s everywhere, and it’s explicitly replacing human art. Gross.

AI music generation is perplexing in the opposite way. Last year, I worried that I would grow equally tired of it. But no! I’m really enjoying some AI music — and so is the rest of the world. The viral San Juan song inspired covers from humans and lip sync videos from “Mila Kunis, Charlie Puth and Jennifer Love Hewitt”. AI has also inspired new genres: I’ve been humming AI is normal technology? (95k views), LGTM (Looks Good to Me) (1.6M), and The Simulation’s Ending (169k) for weeks. As one commenter wrote on OMG! We’ve found other agents (120k):

I think AI art & music are beautiful when they are used as lenses for human creativity, rather than replacements for it. I guessed something similar last year, and I think last year’s music proved me right. As soon as commercialism replaced creativity, I was out. I soured on Eiden XII when they started sharing new “but it hits different” covers weekly, and I got bored of steel coils-style edutainment after hearing the first clone. There’s something cynical and manipulative about a synthetic woman belting “talk me out of dying” when some dude (presumably) makes money every time I play it.

Similarly, I haven’t listened to any of the new Doompop that’s hit my feed. It’s cool when you generate a few songs; less cool when you post every day. It feels like vultures picking ad revenue from the corpse of a good idea.

That is evident in the world of video generation. I largely escaped last year (although my mom got some weird whale-cleaning videos), but now I’m seeing a bunch. I see AI ads all the time — most memorably with horrid horse-people in Sixt ads. I got baited into a video of a fake Edna Mode lookalike & some slop WW2 history videos, and my wife got tricked by AI summaries of Adventure Time marketed as sleep aids. All of them hoping to get views, to get ad revenue, to get — as Corridor Digital puts it—“a little bit skimmed off of that YouTube trough.” It is sobering to open an AI history video in Incognito and gaze at the misleading slop recommended next to it:

It is horrid to see these machines that can mass-produce art being used to mass-produce art. And I know that seems silly, but there’s a world where we use these tools to elevate artists, just like coding agents elevate me.

I am lucky I do not make my living from art. Art remains valuable to me. Even if AI can write a song faster than I can, I still doodle, I still play piano.

Drawin' it yourself is more fun, anyway.

UsefulnessNotesImage generation❌A net negative so farMusic generation👍I like it when it’s non-commercialVideo generation❌Has it ever been used for good?
Conclusion

So here we are, 12 months later.

12 months since my first abortive attempts to have agents write code. 10 months since Claude Code first made me say, “wow,” when it built me an insurance comparison tool in one shot. And now machines write 90%+ of my code.

It is easy to forget how new this is. 15 months ago, AI did well at a prestigious high school math competition. 2 months ago, AI solved Navier-Stokes.

Last year, I wrote: “I’m confident we’re just starting to see what AI can achieve.” That remains true. We are just now beginning to see what these mechanized coders and mathematicians can build. My friends have built each other tools to communicate. I was able to finally clean up and share a tool I’d started in 2020. Agents helped me finish up an open-source change I’d wanted to make for years, start making an app, test massive changes to old software, and quickly understand new operating systems.

That is just the start.

It is a brave new world. Where these machines also ship corporate slop and leave mathematicians in shock. But I think of how my uncle uses these tools to build his own software; how my friends make software that helps us stay in touch; how these things have helped me learn so, so much. Tools can be used to help people.

That is how I hope to use AI.

Thanks to Peter Kreiseder and Atherai Maran for consulting. Claude helped make the status icon look more Claude-y.

Want next year's article? (and others in between)No spam. Just an email for new posts.Appendix: my subscriptions

In case you’re wondering, I’m subscribed to:

Claude Pro ($17/mo)GitHub Copilot Pro ($10/mo)

I cancelled OpenAI about a month ago, which is crazy. OpenAI was my first AI subscription! But most of my personal usage is Claude Code, and I ended up using Claude for random questions instead of ChatGPT. And last year we thought OpenAI was so far ahead!

I use GitHub Copilot Pro solely for autocomplete.

item.title: Show HN: Uncracked City, detective game where you question LLM suspects that lie
item.description:
Salem, the morning after Halloween. Meg Ashcombe, the last of her family, lies at the foot of her grand staircase, one slipper on the thirteenth step, the front door bolted from inside. Half the town says the Grey Captain finally took her.

Every case happens in a real neighbourhood. Find the clues, open what is locked.

02

Question the suspects

Ask your own questions, typed or spoken, in any of the game's six languages. Each suspect answers in their own voice. Some of them lie.

03

Catch the lie, then report

Hold a clue against a statement. When the lie cracks, write your report: three tries, not one more.

A world tour to learn. Then the real cases.

Paris, Rio de Janeiro, Marrakech, Tokyo, Sydney: five training levels, each harder than the last. Then come the real cases, harder still. Each one shows how many investigators have solved it. For most of them: nobody. Not yet.

Nobody has solved it yet

One city, one secret

The first time you open a case, you fly there across the map. Solve it, and its city is stamped in your passport.

Venice

Lisbon

Edinburgh

Amsterdam

Cusco

Seoul

Cape Town

New York

Help and contact

A question, a bug, a suspect's line that goes wrong: write to us. In the game, “Flag” under a line sends it to us directly.

The game is played without an account. To erase everything: Settings → “Start over” → “Erase everything”. Without the phone that created your player, write to us.

item.title: Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3
item.description:
Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode

We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark.

In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright. Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web.

You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’.

For websites that signal support of dark mode with <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark.

How does Adaptive Dark Mode work?

At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged.

While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio. Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark.

Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear.

It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos.

Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, <canvas> content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict.

It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformations with great speed and power efficiency, all while rigorously protecting user privacy.

Making your site work even better

In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices.

If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding.

Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles.

Building your own dark mode

For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been easier.

All the web technology needed to fully support dark mode is widely available today, including:

Newer CSS functions like color-mix() and contrast-color(), plus popular techniques for organizing design systems with CSS variables provide additional options and flexibility.

Be sure to declare dark mode support using the color-scheme meta tag in your HTML head and/or by setting the color-scheme property on :root or body in your CSS. Don’t wait to inject this information later via JavaScript. This best practice helps ensure your site is rendered correctly as fast as possible.

Using the “light only” color scheme

If you would like your web app or website to not be transformed by Adaptive Dark Mode, you can communicate this using color-scheme. The HTML <meta name="color-scheme" content="light only"> tag lets browsers know that 1) this page supports light mode and 2) should only be displayed in light mode. The color-scheme: light only rule does the same thing, but with the flexibility of CSS, allowing you to just target specific elements on the page — or of course, you can target the whole page with :root { }. (Note: the ‘only’ keyword is not supported in Safari 27.3 beta 1. Check back as Adaptive Dark Mode evolves through the beta process.)

Protecting user privacy

Apple firmly believes user privacy is a fundamental human right. If websites could detect when a user has enabled Adaptive Dark Mode, that would increase the amount of fingerprintable information and weaken privacy protections against trackers.

As a result, Safari prevents websites from detecting when Adaptive Dark Mode has been applied. JavaScript that queries CSS colors will get the original authored colors, not the transformed ones. Any images drawn into canvas render in their original form.

Feedback

item.title: C++26 Disapproved
item.description:
C++26 DIS failed, how does C++ survive?

On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved!

I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views.

The Current Status

As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote.

In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures, there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved.

The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release.

The Process

Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree.

However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently.

The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026.

It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me.

The History of Contracts in C++

The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote.

In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes.

And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached.

What happens next?

The big problem: what happens next? ISO, of course, has a process for this. It offers various options:

Submit a revised draft for a new DIS vote. Submit a revised draft to the committee (that would be the CD phase). Publish a revised draft as a Technical Specification. Cancel the project.

All of these possibilities mean a delay in the next C++ standard. Whether it will still be called C++26 is also up in the air, but that’s a much smaller issue.

The difficulty with all four options is that they require a majority within WG21. However, this working group voted to move C++26 with Contracts into the next voting phase leading to its release. And it did so with more than just the required two-thirds majority. The feature didn’t come out of nowhere, either; it was developed over the course of years through the work and possibly personal commitment of many people. It’s hard to imagine that this group would simply want to abandon its work, which has received approval on multiple occasions so far. The same applies to the group that is dissatisfied with Contracts. This group, too, has invested effort, in some cases even in alternative implementations. It’s hard to imagine that, after these groups voted “no” in the DIS vote, the result would change without Contracts being removed.

Even the last option removing C++26 requires a majority in WG21. As I understand it, this step would mean reverting to C++23 and proceeding to C++29 without a single change. This would affect the work of even more people. WG21 would then be tasked with incorporating features that have already been successfully included in C++26 into C++29. Since this can only be done through a paper backed by at least one person advocating for it, features could be omitted if that person lacks the motivation or time.

Of course, certainty about the voting outcome can only be achieved if the respective path is actually taken.

Unfortunately, the way forward is currently more than uncertain. Perhaps this also explains why ISO/IEC DIS 26926 marked the end of this activity. Consensus is needed to move forward. Trust is always required for consensus. Unfortunately, that trust has just been shaken.

The next C++ standard, and thus the future of C++, is currently at an impasse.

The good news is that the next meeting will take place on November 16, which is just a few days away. The top priority will be to break the deadlock. This will very likely have implications for C++29 as well; in fact, there is currently no reason to continue working on this project.

My Personal Opinion

Normally, my articles are technically focused and free of personal opinion. Regarding the rejected DIS, I can only say that I consider it a massive disaster and feel sorry for the entire C++ community. Regardless of whether someone likes Contracts, considers them important, or sees major weaknesses in them, the topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting “no,” an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken. Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes. Overall, the result is one in which all participants have given their best. During the DIS vote, the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust.

Andreas

Arrows to arrows, categories to queries (2025)
item.description:
Arrows to Arrows, Categories to Queries

I’ve had a little time off of work as of late, and been spending it in characteristically unwise ways. In particular, I’ve written a little programming language that compiles to SQL. I call it catlang. That’s not to say that I’ve written a new query language. It’s a programming language, whose compiler spits out one giant SELECT statement. When you run that query in postgres, you get the output of your program.

Why have I done this? Because I needed a funny compilation target to test out the actual features of the language, which is that its intermediary language is a bunch of abstract category theory nonsense. Which I’ll get to. But I’m sure you first want to see this bad boy in action.

Behold, the function that returns 100 regardless of what input you give it. But it does it with the equivalent of a while loop:

count : Int -> Int count = x -> loop x i -> n <- join id id -< i z <- abs . (-) -< (n, 100) case z of inl _ -> inr . (+) -< (n, 1) inr _ -> inl -< n

If you’re familiar with arrow notation, you’ll notice the above looks kinda like one big proc block. This is not a coincidence (because nothing is a coincidence). I figured if I were to go through all of this work, we might as well get a working arrow desugarer out of the mix. But I digress; that’s a story for another time.

Anyway, what’s going on here is we have an arrow count, which takes a single argument x. We then loop, starting from the value of x. Inside the loop, we now have a new variable i, which we do some voodoo on to compute n—the current value of the loop variable. Then we subtract 100 from n, and take the absolute value. The abs function here is a bit odd; it returns Left (abs x) if the input was negative, and Right x otherwise. Then we branch on the output of abs, where Left and Right have been renamed inl and inr respectively. If n - 100 was less than zero, we find ourselves in the inl case, where we add 1 to n and wrap the whole thing in inr—which the loop interprets as “loop again with this new value.” Otherwise, n - 100 was non-negative, and so we can return n directly.

Is it roundabout? You bet! The obtuseness here is not directly a feature, I was just looking for conceptually simple things I could do which would be easy to desugar into category-theoretical stuff. Which brings us to the intermediary language. After desugaring the source syntax for count above, we’re left with this IL representation:

We’ll discuss all of this momentarily, but for now, just let your eyes glaze over the pretty unicode.

The underlying idea here is that each of these remaining symbols has very simple and specific algebraic semantics. It’s not pretty, rather amazingly, running the above query in postgres 17 will in fact return a single row with a single column whose value is 100. And you’d better believe it does it by actually looping its way up to 100. If you don’t believe me, make the following change:

- SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC LIMIT 1) + SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC)

which will instead return a row for each step of the iteration.

There are some obvious optimizations I could make to the generated SQL, but it didn’t seem worth my time, since that’s not the interesting part of the project.

What the Hell Is Going On?

Let’s take some time to discuss the underlying category theory here. I am by no means an expert, but what I have learned after a decade of bashing my head against this stuff is that a little goes a long way.

For our intents and purposes, we have types, and arrows (functions) between types. We always have the identity “do nothing arrow” id:

id :: a ~> a

and we can compose arrows by lining up one end to another:1

(⨟) :: (a ~> b) -> (b ~> c) -> (a ~> c)

Unlike Haskell (or really any programming language, for that matter), we DO NOT have the notion of function application. That is, there is no arrow:

-- doesn't exist! ($) :: (a ~> b) -> a -> b

You can only compose arrows, you can’t apply them. That’s why we call these things “arrows” rather than “functions.”

There are a bundle of arrows for working with product types. The two projection functions correspond to fst and snd, taking individual components out of pairs:

prj₁ :: (a, b) ~> a prj₂ :: (a, b) ~> b

How do we get things into pairs in the first place? We can use the “fork” operation, which takes two arrows computing b and c, and generates a new arrow which generates a pair of (b, c):

(△) :: (a ~> b) -> (a ~> c) -> (a ~> (b, c))

If you’re coming from a Haskell background, it’s tempting to think of this operation merely as the (,) pair constructor. But you’ll notice from the type of the computation that there can be no data dependency between b and c, thus we are free to parallelize each side of the pair.

In category theory, the distinction between left and right sides of an arrow is rather arbitrary. This gives rise to a notion called duality where we can flip the arrows around, and get cool new behavior. If we dualize all of our product machinery, we get the coproduct machinery, where a coproduct of a and b is “either a or b, but definitely not both nor neither.”

Swapping the arrow direction of prj₁ and prj₂, and replacing (,) with Either gives us the following injections:

inl :: a ~> Either a b inr :: b ~> Either a b

and the following “join” operation for eliminating coproducts:

(▽) :: (a ~> c) -> (b ~> c) -> (Either a b ~> c)

Again, coming from Haskell this is just the standard either function. It corresponds to a branch between one of two cases.

As you can see, with just these eight operations, we already have a tremendous amount of expressivity. We can express data dependencies via ⨟ and branching via ▽. With △ we automatically encode opportunities for parallelism, and gain the ability to build complicated data structures, with prj₁ and prj₂ allowing us to get the information back out of the data structures.

You’ll notice in the IL that there are no variable names anywhere to be found. The desugaring of the source language builds a stack (via the something to allocate △ id pattern), and replaces subsequent variable lookups with a series of projections on the stack to find the value again. On one hand, this makes the categorical IL rather hard to read, but it makes it very easy to re-target! Many domains do have a notion of grouping, but don’t have a native notion of naming.

For example, in an electronic circuit, I can have a ribbon of 32 wires which represents an Int32. If I have another ribbon of 32 wires, I can trivially route both wires into a 64-wire ribbon corresponding to a pair of (Int32, Int32).

By eliminating names before we get to the IL, it means no compiler backend ever needs to deal with names. They can just work on a stack representation, and are free to special-case optimize series of projections if they are able to.

Of particular interest to this discussion is how we desugar loops in catlang. The underlying primitive is cochoice:

cochoice :: (Either a c ~> Either b c) -> (a ~> b)

which magically turns an arrow on Eithers into an arrow without the eithers. We obviously must run that arrow on eithers. If that function returns inl, then we’re happy and we can just output that. But if the function returns inr, we have no choice but to pass it back in to the eithered arrow. In Haskell, cochoice is implemented as:

cochoiceHask :: (Either a c -> Either b c) -> a -> c cochoiceHask f = go . Left where go :: Either a c -> b go eac = case f eac of Left b -> b Right c -> go (Right c)

which as you can see, will loop until f finally returns a Left. What’s neat about this formulation of a loop is that we can statically differentiate between our first and subsequent passes through the loop body. The first time through eac is Left, while for all other times it is Right. We don’t take advantage of it in the original count program, but how many times have you written loop code that needs to initialize something its first time through?

Compiling to SQL

So that’s the underlying theory behind the IL. How can we compile this to SQL now?

As alluded to before, we simply need to give SQL implementations for each of the operations in the intermediary language. As a simple example, id compiles to SELECT * FROM {}, where {} is the input of the arrow.

The hardest part here was working out a data representation. It seems obvious to encode each element of a product as a new column, but what do we do about coproducts? After much work thought, I decided to flatten out the coproducts. So, for example, the type:

(Int, Either Int Int)

would be represented as three columns:

( f1 INT NOT NULL , f2 INT , f3 INT )

with the constraint that exactly one of f2 or f3 would be IS NOT NULL at any given point in time.

With this hammered out, almost everything else is pretty trivial. Composition corresponds to a nested query. Forks are CROSS JOINs which concatenate the columns of each sub-query. Joins are UNIONs, where we add a WHERE field IS NOT NULL clause to enforce we’re looking at the correct coproduct constructor.

Cochoice is the only really tricky thing, but it corresponds to a recursive CTE. Generating a recursive CTE table for the computation isn’t too hard, but getting the final value out of it was surprisingly tricky. The semantics of SQL tables is that they are multisets and come with an arbitrary greatest element. Which is to say, you need an column structured in a relevant way in order to query the final result. Due to some quirks in what postgres accepts, and in how I structured my queries, it was prohibitively hard to insert a “how many times have I looped” column and order by that. So instead I cheated and added a clock_timestamp() as step column which looks at the processor clock and ordered by that.

This is clearly a hack, and presumably will cause problems if I ever add some primitives which generate more than one row, but again, this is just for fun and who cares. Send me a pull request if you’re offended by my chicanery!

Stupid Directions To Go In the Future

I’ve run out of vacation time to work on this project, so I’m probably not going to get around to the meta-circular stupidity I was planning.

The compiler still needs a few string-crunching primitives (which are easy to add), but then it would be simple to write a little brainfuck interpreter in catlang. Which I could then compile to SQL. Now we’ve got a brainfuck interpreter running in postgres. Of course, this has been done by hand before, but to my knowledge, never via compilation.

There exist C to brainfuck compilers. And postgres is written in C. So in a move that would make Xzibit proud, we could run postgres in postgres. And of course, it would be fun to run brainfuck in brainfuck. That’d be a cool catlang backend if someone wanted to contribute such a thing.

Notes and Due Diligence and What Have You

I am not the first person to do anything like this. The source language of catlang is heavily inspired by Haskell’s arrow syntax, which in turn is essentially a desugaring algorithm for Arrows. Arrows are slightly the wrong abstraction because they require an operation arr :: (a -> b) -> (a ~> b)—which requires you to be able to embed Haskell functions in your category, something which is almost never possible.

Unfortunately, arrow syntax in Haskell desugars down to arr for almost everything it does, which in turn makes arrow notation effectively useless. In an ideal world, everything I described in this blog post would be a tiny little Haskell library, with arrow notation doing the heavy lifting. But that is just not the world we live in.

Nor am I the first person to notice that there are categorical semantics behind programming languages. I don’t actually know whom to cite on this one, but it is well-established folklore that the lambda calculus corresponds to cartesian-closed categories. The “closed” part of “cartesian-closed” means we have an operation eval :: (a ~> b, a) ~> b, but everyone and their dog has implemented the lambda calculus, so I thought it would be fun to see how far we can get without it. This is not a limitation on catlang’s turing completeness (since cochoice gives us everything we need.)

I’ve been thinking about writing a category-first programming language for the better part of a decade, ever since I read Compiling to Categories. That paper takes Haskell and desugars it back down to categories. I stole many of the tricks here from that paper.

Anyway. All of the code is available on github if you’re interested in taking a look. The repo isn’t up to my usual coding standards, for which you have my apologies. Of note is the template-haskell backend which can spit out Haskell code; meaning it wouldn’t be very hard to make a quasiquoter to compile catlang into what Haskell’s arrow desugaring ought to be. If there’s enough clamor for such a thing, I’ll see about turning this part into a library.

When looking at the types of arrows in this essay, we make the distinction that ~> are arrows that we can write in catlang, while -> exist in the metatheory.↩︎

item.title: Distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in young patients
item.description:
Study reveals distinct cellular and genetic differences in colorectal cancer in younger patients Researchers identified age-associated differences in tumor composition and gene activity, creating a foundation for investigating why colorectal cancer can be more aggressive in younger adults

Dana-Farber Cancer Institute researchers, along with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation, and the Broad Institute, have uncovered biological clues to why colorectal cancer can behave more aggressively in younger people. Published today in Nature Medicine, the study — the largest of its kind — lays a foundation for understanding age-associated differences in colorectal cancer and exploring future treatments.

In the United States, colorectal cancer diagnosis rates among people younger than 50 rose 2.9% per year from 2013 through 2022, according to the American Cancer Society. Its 2026 report identifies colorectal cancer as the leading cause of cancer death in this age group. Younger patients are also more likely to be diagnosed at advanced stages, underscoring the need to better understand the biology of early-onset disease.

"Through Dana-Farber’s Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center, we see how profoundly this disease can affect younger patients and their families, often during the busiest and most formative years of life," said co-senior author Kimmie Ng, MD, MPH, who is the director of the Young-Onset Colorectal Cancer Center at Dana-Farber. "This collaborative work with Mass General Brigham researchers from the Gene Lay Institute and researchers from the Broad Institute gives us important new insight into the biology of these tumors. The findings provide a valuable roadmap for further investigating the distinct features of young-onset colorectal cancer. Our ultimate goal is to discover novel strategies for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment for our young patients."

"The need to understand why colorectal cancer is affecting younger adults at increasing rates is urgent," said co-senior author Ana C. Anderson, PhD, a core faculty member of the Gene Lay Institute of Immunology and Inflammation at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Massachusetts General Hospital, and Harvard Medical School. "And that starts with understanding the biology of the disease across the entire lifespan. By looking beyond conventional age cutoffs, we’ve uncovered biological patterns that earlier studies may have missed and created a foundation for the field to investigate them further. While we’re still at the beginning of understanding what these differences mean, our work gives researchers a new direction to pursue in tackling this urgent problem in human disease."

The research team, led by first author Caroline Porter, PhD, of the Klarman Cell Observatory at the Broad Institute, studied specimens from surgeries stored in Dana-Farber’s Gastrointestinal Biobank from surgeries at Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Co-senior authors include Anderson, Ng, and Ramnik J. Xavier, MD, PhD, of the Broad Institute, Mass General Brigham, and the Gene Lay Institute. They analyzed 189 tumors from patients ages 29 to 90+, including 54 diagnosed before age 50, and 135 diagnosed at age 50 or older. Using a technique called single-nucleus RNA sequencing, the researchers measured gene activity in more than 850,000 cancer cells and other cells in the tumors. The technique, which works with frozen tissue, enabled the team to build a detailed map of tumor cells by studying archived samples with extensive clinical record data.

Rather than dividing the tumor samples into two data sets and comparing the younger and older age groups, the researchers looked for factors that changed gradually with age, accounting for tumor location, stage, sex, and prior treatment in their analyses. This approach revealed subtle differences that likely would have been obscured by a simple two-data set comparison.

Among tumors of the most common colorectal cancer subtype, younger patients’ tumors had a significantly higher proportion of connective and supporting cells relative to cancer cells. A higher proportion of connective and supporting cells has been linked to chemotherapy resistance in several types of solid cancer. The team confirmed this pattern using gene-activity data from 564 other tumors and computer analysis of stained tissue images from another 712 tumors.

Younger patients also had higher activity of long non-coding RNAs, molecules that can regulate genes without making proteins. Some appeared repeatedly across different types of cancer cells. Many are "dark" RNAs, whose functions remain largely unknown. The team also saw gene activity suggesting stronger signaling between cells that can help cancer cells move and invade nearby tissue in younger patients.

"Our study is an advance from previous work in that we analyzed tumors from a large number of patients and used single-cell approaches to find novel features unique to tumors from young patients," said Xavier, a co-senior author of the study, a core institute member at the Broad Institute, Kurt Isselbacher Professor at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, and Vice Director of the Gene Lay Institute. Xavier is also a gastroenterologist at Mass General Brigham. "This work sets the stage for future mechanistic studies on how these cell programs interact with chemicals from the diet and from gut microbes to cause early-onset colorectal cancer."

Although the findings provide key insight into colorectal cancer in young individuals, they do not yet provide proof that these differences cause more aggressive disease. One remaining question is whether there are differences in immune responses in these tumors across ages — the researchers' methods captured relatively few immune cells. Future studies will explore how these changes may affect cancer growth and spread, and whether they offer opportunities for prevention or treatment.

item.title: The lost malloc()
item.description:
The lost malloc()

(Sorry, I couldn't resist not putting a catchy title :)

Prompted by another project idea that popped into my mind, I did some Unix archaeology and looked at the original sources. This is the most fun I've ever had reading someone else's code - probably due to the historical significance. But also because of how delightfully approachable it was, compared to modern monstrocities.

This is a short(-ish) post regarding how they handled the mundane and boring task of allocating and managing memory (in C). In the future I'd like to read more about Unix the OS, its design, architecture & implementation.

A long time ago...

In a PDP far, far away, our journey begins with the fourth edition of Unix, released November '73, more than half a century ago. C actually first appeared in the second edition, released the year before, but wasn't extensively used. V4 is special because even the majority of the kernel was written in (let's call it "medieval") C by that point. The system had grown, however, and it was quite capable. You'll find that many Unix things we have today in POSIX-land were already present in V4.

Super fun fact: A tape containing V4 was only found last year! Previously, it was thought to be completely lost to time.

Linear allocation

The first interesting bit is found among the C "compiler" sources. In quotes, because it wasn't a monolithic compiler as we know it today. Rather, it was a set of distinct tools which you chained in order to get an object file from C code.

In /usr/c/c20.c:814, from what I can gather a very primitive optimiser, if you will (referred to as "C object code improver" in V5; there aren't many comments in V4) you see:

alloc(an) { register int n; register char *p; n = an; n++; n =& ~01; if (lasta+n >= lastr) { if (sbrk(2000) == -1) { write(2, "Out of space\n", 14); exit(1); } lastr =+ 2000; } p = lasta; lasta =+ n; return(p); }

Isn't that fascinating? This routine is used throughout the program to allocate memory. And if you squint, this is just a linear allocator. It aligns the size, checks if the region is big enough, otherwise tries to extend it. On failure, it just cold-exits. Which means callers don't have to check for NULL every single time, and indeed they do not.

The "region" isn't named, unlike how you'd do it today with arenas. However, the above does have a nice property, in that by using sbrk(), when we extend the heap, no pointer is invalidated.

And they don't bother freeing memory, because why would they? There's no need. Everything exists for the lifetime of the program.

dmr/malloc

This is the most interesting bit in my opinion, and the reason why I chose that title.

In Dennis' directory, you find a file named malloc.c. And you see two functions there:

struct map { char *m_size; char *m_addr; }; malloc(mp, size) struct map *mp; mfree(mp, size, aa) struct map *mp;

Seems familiar? Yep, it's mfree() with an m. These functions obviously deal with memory (de)allocation, and are the precursor to the ones we're familiar with today. But, the interfaces are different.

malloc() receives an additional first argument called mp (for "map"), and so does mfree(). What is that? Well, let's see how they're used:

p = malloc(coremap, sizeof foo); ... mfree(coremap, sizeof foo, p); q = malloc(swapmap, sizeof bar); ... mfree(swapmap, sizeof bar, q);

So, they pass in some objects coremap and swapmap. What are those? From /usr/sys/systm.h:2:

int coremap[CMAPSIZ]; int swapmap[SMAPSIZ];

They're just flat memory regions! So these malloc() and mfree() work on explicit memory regions! Not only that, mfree() receives the size of the object it is deallocating, as it should. Those are just infinitely-times better interfaces than traditional malloc()/free().

Imagine using a library that has such an interface. You could deallocate all its memory resources by just discarding the entire region you delegated to it. Heap corruption bugs would be less severe because you could partition memory. You could trivially limit the amount of memory third party code allocates. The list goes on and on...

(Side note: They slightly messed up here and the regions should've been sized CMAPSIZ/2 and SMAPSIZ/2 respectively. They did fix that later.)

However, I don't think all these benefits were in the minds of Dennis and Ken. So why did they go with that interface and why did they partition memory to "core" and "swap"? The reason is, I believe, just hardware constraints. These interfaces stay like that up to V6 (maybe V7 too?), released the spring of '75, and thankfully there's an infamously good resource about that edition.

From A Commentary on the Sixth Edition UNIX Operating System by John Lions:

These are concerned with the allocation and subsequent release of two kinds of memory resources, namely:

main memory in units of 32 words (64 bytes); disk swap area in units of 256 words (512 bytes).

For each of these two kinds of resource, a list of available areas is maintained within a resource "map" (either "coremap" or "swapmap"). A pointer to the appropriate resource "map" is always passed to "malloc" and "mfree" so that the routines themselves do not have to know the kind of resource with which they are dealing.

And it goes on to explain how the underlying allocation algorithm works. These do not do linear allocation (hence the mfree()). Basically, it's a list of blocks (struct map), ordered by address, where you do first-fit and also coalesce neighbour blocks.

The sixth edition is also the first where the term "arena" appears, in /usr/source/s4/alloc.s:17:

/char *allocs[2] { /*initial empty arena*/ Rolling back

... to the topic of linear allocation... In V6's /usr/source/s1/diff1.c:88, I think the first ever version of diff(1), you find:

char *area; char *top; alloc(n) { register char *p; p = area; n = (n+1) & ~1; area =+ n; while(area > top) { if(sbrk(1024) == -1) { mesg("Out of space\n"); exit(1); } top =+ 1024; } return(p); }

This is not all that much different from the previous alloc(), but this time it handles any allocation size. It uses a while to continue extending the region and stops when enough space has been reserved. The actual interesting part happens later, at unsort():143:

unsort(f, l, b) struct line *f; int *b; { int *a; int i; a = alloc((l+1)*sizeof(a[0])); for(i=1;i<=l;i++) a[f[i].serial] = f[i].value; for(i=1;i<=l;i++) b[i] = a[i]; area = a; }

I'm not exactly sure what that function does, but it doesn't matter. What matters is that they allocate some memory (a = alloc(...);), then roll back the region (area = a;)! Though they subsequently just copy it to b, so it seems like this was redundant.

Computing sizes

Most of the code directly calls malloc()/alloc() and friends, and inlines the size computation logic. Like the line we saw earlier:

a = alloc((l+1)*sizeof(a[0]));

I don't do that anymore, and neither should you! I use a couple macros akin to C++'s new that handle all the sizeof business. But I am a dumb-dumb. Surely these guys must've come across the same pain points, and, if so, what did they do? Let's jump to V7, released January '79, four years after V6. You find this macro:

#define ALLOC(x) (struct x *) ckalloc(sizeof(struct x))

where they use it like:

struct foo { ... }; p = ALLOC(foo);

Nice! It's interesting to note where you find it; In /usr/src/cmd/f77/defines:38 and /usr/src/cmd/make/defs:38. Slightly suspicious. The former is part of the Fortran 77 compiler and latter of make. Stuart Feldman is the person who worked on both of those programs! It's clear that multiple people were working on the system at that time. A macro like that isn't used in any other program, sadly.

V7 is the first edition where you also find the assert() macro, and it was used extensively back then too. Good job! They also significantly expanded the number of man pages. Fun fact: I did $ man V7/usr/man/man3/foo.3 -- on 47 year old pages -- and it worked first try absolutely fine.

Let's go to V8, released in February '85, four years before the first C standard. You find this wild macro in /usr/src/cmd/ideal/memut.c:7:

char *fooalloc; #define tryalloc(new,kind) \ if (!(new =(kind *) malloc(sizeof (kind)))) {\ emergency ();\ if (!(new =(kind *) malloc(sizeof (kind)))) {\ fprintf (stderr, "ideal: Out of space\n");\ exit (1);\ }\ };\ for (fooalloc = (char *) new;\ fooalloc < ((char *) new) + sizeof (kind);\ fooalloc ++)\ *fooalloc = '\0';

If someone is too harsh because you used macros, point them at the above. Usage is bit different this time:

struct foo *x; tryalloc(x, struct foo);

I decided to include it because the macro zero-initialises by default whatever was allocated! You also see a more familiar-looking malloc() being used. It appears this is the edition that they switched to the more traditional malloc()/free() interfaces we know. I'll hypothesize why that is at the very end.

But it gets even more interesting. In V8 you also find these macros:

#define new(type) ((type *) alloc (sizeof (type))) #define new(t) ((t *) alloc (sizeof (t))) #define new(s) (s *)alloc(sizeof (s))

When I saw these definitions I jumped out of my chair. It's basically how I'd define it too! You'll find them in:

/usr/src/cmd/finddev.c:245, part of finddev(8). /usr/src/cmd/asd/asd.h:13, part of asd(8). /usr/include/ic.h:55, part of *checks notes* I have no idea.

respectively.

Unfortunately, I can't find the author(s) of any of these.

Cfront

In V8, you'll also find Cfront, a.k.a. medieval C++. It's then reasonable to assume that Stroustrup was inspired by the above macros and decided to incorporate new as a language-level feature. However, in A History of C++: 1979−1991, he writes:

In Simula, it is not possible to have local or global variables of class types; that is, every object of a class must be allocated on the free store using the new operator.

Huh. So C++'s new was inspired by the programming language "Simula". It's fair to say that the macros above were likely also derived from there. But Simula was quite old even by the 70s, let alone 1985. Perhaps Stroustrup persuaded people, or wrote those macros himself. He later writes:

The new operator that both allocates memory from the free store and invokes a constructor to ensure initialization was borrowed from Simula. The delete operator was a necessary complement because I did not want C with Classes to depend on a garbage collector. The argument for the new operator can be summarized like this. Would you rather write:

X* p = new X(2);

or

struct X * p = (struct X *) malloc(sizeof(struct X)); if (p == 0) error("memory exhausted"); p−>init(2);

and which version are you most likely to make a mistake in? The arguments against -- which were voiced quite a lot at the time -- were "but we don’t really need it," and "but someone will have used new as an identifier." Both observations are correct, of course. Introducing operator new thus made the use of free store more convenient and less error−prone. This increased its use even further so that the C free store allocation routine malloc() used to implement new became the most common performance bottleneck in real systems. [...] Having real programs spend 50% or more of their time in malloc() wasn’t acceptable.

(emphasis mine :P)

He makes a compelling argument, which I agree with, but doesn't mention the new() macros that basically did the same thing. Although you'll find many programs in V8 that do the latter, verbose thing. Now I want to know the author(s) of those macros even more!

Sims

This is a big parentheses because I wanted to know how Simula came up with new. Wikipedia states:

Simula 67 introduced objects, classes, inheritance and subclasses, virtual procedures, coroutines, and discrete event simulation, and featured garbage collection.

And it appeared in 1967. Wow! In the 1964 report of SIMULA I, you'll find:

[...] The symbol "new" only serves to resolve an ambiguity of the identifier A inside the activity blah blah blah [...]. Elsewhere the symbol new is redundant, but can often be used to advantage to improve readability.

So it was only used to resolve grammar ambiguities (I think?). And Stroustrup re-purposed it. Clever!

Further reading

The History of Simula, by Jan Rune Holmevik. Reads like (bad) Sci-Fi. All the politics nonsense aside, what I found most curious is that they completely specified the language before attempting to write a compiler for it. They started writing the first compiler atleast a year after. This would sound insane today, but I guess the cost of writing code was substantially higher back then.

Also: The development of the SIMULA languages, by the authors. I didn't read that one, although I should...

It's honestly amazing how influential Simula was. In "10.5 Operating Instruction" they even use the term "run time system" and give it the same meaning we're accustomed to.

Simula, in turn, was partly inspired by SIMSCRIPT (don't laugh). If you skim its 1962 report, you won't find a mention of new. You'll however find CREATE:

When a new Entity is created by a CREATE statement, space for storing its Attribute values is allocated in the amount specified on the Definition Form. This record is given an identification number, and the Variable specified in the CREATE statement is automatically set equal to this number.

For example, the statement "CREATE DOG CALLED FIDO" allocates the required amount of storage for the Attributes of a DOG, and sets FIDO equal to the identification number of the Attribute record.

Fascinating. The whole SIMSCRIPT report is fascinating actually, and I only briefly skimmed through it. At the beginning, it even describes something like a primitive ECS, by my understanding. At the end though it slaps you back to reality:

and you remember what year it was.

Later editions

In V9's /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:14, part of the Sam editor by Rob Pike, you find a "generalised" version of new():

#define new(t, n) ((t *)alloc(((ulong)(n)*sizeof(t))))

Although, by and large, almost every program doesn't do this. Most just directly call malloc() and friends, and do size calculations \w error checking at every call site. I don't know why, considering how much error-prone that is, but maybe due to inertia. It's a similar story in V10, but I didn't check it as thoroughly since it's quite big (it includes medieval GCC!).

So what happened?

They were so close to arenas; with linear allocation and explicit memory regions, rolling back, and even having a nice new() macro. All this is speculation at this point, but maybe some of it is correct. First of all, most programs had trivial object lifetimes. Allocate memory, read some data, process/crunch and spit out some result. You don't need any disciplined memory allocation strategy for that. You can even use malloc() for everything and let the OS reclaim it once the process exits. Given how simple malloc() was at first, it wouldn't be much of a bottleneck either. The philosophy of programs only "doing a single thing well" also fitted this pattern.

Secondly, it's clear some decisions were motivated by the very little memory they had to play with. And there was no virtual memory either (initially, that is). Nowadays, you can "allocate" however big of a memory region you want and all will probably be okay. They couldn't really do that, so they were fighting to reclaim every empty block and gap there was and scale a program's space with how much is actually needed. There's a counterpoint to this, however, because some code is confused. Sometimes you see fixed-size buffers/arrays pop up, seemingly out of nowhere, and the program bail out if they fill. I'm not sure why, but perhaps they didn't deem it worthwhile the complexity to use malloc() in those cases and/or "don't fix it if it ain't broke" kind-of thing.

And clearly, when they could get away with simple linear allocation, they did so.

Thirdly, I suspect they had grown tired of doing any manual memory management at all. Dropping explicit memory regions from the malloc() interface is a change that, on the surface, simplifies stuff even further. You make the implementation-side smarter and you don't have to worry about passing coremap or swapmap or anymap. Remember: the way programs and problems were approached didn't lead to complex object lifetimes. And when you had to deal with tangled lifetimes, malloc()/free() appear deceivably simple in the beginning.

That last point seems more "vibes" than evidence, but there is some evidence actually. In V7 they added galloc(3):

GALLOC(3) GALLOC(3) NAME galloc, gfree, garbage - storage allocation with garbage collection SYNOPSIS char *galloc(n) unsigned n; gfree(p) char *p; garbage( ) DESCRIPTION These functions perform heap storage allocation with garbage collection. Galloc allocates a block of at least n bytes and returns a pointer to it. Gfree frees a block previously allocated by galloc. When space gets tight, garbage blocks are freed automati- cally. A block allocated by galloc is deemed to be garbage unless it is reachable. A reachable block is one whose first byte is pointed to by a declared C variable or by a pointer in a reachable block.

and Rob Pike had this in /jtools/src/sam/sam.h:15:

#define gcnew(p, n) ((void)gcalloc((ulong)(n)*sizeof((p)[0]), (long **)&(p)))

Ha, myth busted! The authors and people closest to C wanted garbage collection. Given how fast computers are -- and the pace of that -- this makes sense. It's even clearer if you look at what they did later with Limbo and Go. They wanted a higher level general purpose language to write programs in. They had C, so they tried to bolt GC on top of that.

Lastly, I should note that many of these problems were largely known, even at the time. In The Standard C library (1992), P. J. Plauger writes:

Allocating and freeing data objects on the heap in arbitrary order inevitably leaves unusable holes between some of the allocated data objects. That too lowers the usable size of the heap.

Don't overreact to this knowledge. Gather related data into a structure and allocate it all at once. That minimizes heap overhead, to be sure, but it is also good programming style. Do not gather unrelated data just to save heap overhead. Similarly, allocate data objects with similar lifetimes all at once, then free them at about the same time. That minimizes heap fragmentation, but it too is good style. Do not advance or defer unrelated heap operations just to minimize fragmentation. The storage allocation functions are an important aid to programming flexibility. Use them as they are intended to be used.

Criticism by yours truly: It's much easier to say "just do the right thing™" than show and provide tools for how to actually do it.

Conclusion

I don't know. Pay attention to good ideas, otherwise they might get lost? (literally in the case of V4, lol) Sounds cheesy.

Also, the "C object code improver" shatters the illusion that C was somehow magically fast. In fact, Ritchie later added an expression optimiser, and they kept extending both in each edition. I think C just wasn't slow, and it was made fast only with engineering effort put into the compiler (and even then, they had to add register because the compiler wasn't that smart either). It probably remained fast because Unix spread quickly and it carried C along with it, so hardware manufacturers adapted to C. There's a nice essay by Mike Pall discussing how modern CPUs try very hard to infer invariants from compiled C code (which the compiler tried very hard to optimise) and the costs associated with that.

At one point, I also want to investigate Inferno and Plan 9 more. Maybe the BSDs too. Until then...

Cya!
